Horayot 3a:12.english: Rav Asi says: And with regard to a ruling, to determine what constitutes the majority of a congregation, one should follow the majority of the residents of Eretz Yisrael alone, as they are the ones who determine this, as it is stated: “And Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God, seven days and seven days, fourteen days” (I Kings 8:65). And we will clarify what is stated in this verse: Since it is written: “And all Israel with him,” if so, why do I need to add: “A great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt”? What does this come to add? Conclude from it: The additional verse comes to teach us that these residents of Eretz Yisrael are called a congregation; but those others who are outside Eretz Yisrael are not called a congregation.

Horayot 3a:13.english: The Gemara continues defining the majority that establishes liability. It is obvious that if those who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling were numerous, i.e., they constituted a majority, and their percentage subsequently diminished, for example, if some of the sinners died and they now constitute a minority of the congregation; that is the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis. They disagree in a mishna (10b) regarding an anointed High Priest or a king who performed an unwitting transgression before assuming their position, and then later assumed that position. According to the Rabbis, since they were laymen when they sinned, they are liable to bring the offering of a layman. Rabbi Shimon holds that if they became aware of their transgression while still laymen, they bring the offering of a layman, but if they became aware of their transgression after they assumed their positions, they are exempt. Accordingly, in this case of a majority whose number diminished, the Rabbis would say that since they sinned while being a majority, they bring an offering. Rabbi Shimon's view is that the matter depends on their status at the time they became aware of the unwitting sin, whether they were a majority or a minority at that time.

Horayot 3a:17.english: A dilemma was raised before the Sages: If the court issued a ruling that forbidden fat is permitted, and a minority of the congregation performed the transgression of eating forbidden fat on the basis of that ruling, and the court reversed its initial decision, but then reversed itself again and issued a ruling that forbidden fat is permitted, and a different minority of the congregation performed the transgression, what is the halakha? The Gemara elaborates: Is it that since there are two disparate experiences of awareness, the first minority does not combine with the second minority, even though the two minorities together would constitute a majority? Or perhaps, since both this transgression and that transgression are the same, eating forbidden fat, the first minority combines with the second minority, and the two minorities together constitute a majority.

Horayot 3a:18.english: And if you say in that case: Since both this transgression and that transgression are the same, eating forbidden fat, the first minority combines with the second minority, then there is another dilemma: In a case where a minority performed a transgression on the basis of the first ruling of the court and ate forbidden fat that is upon the stomach, and a minority performed a transgression on the basis of the second ruling of the court and ate forbidden fat that is upon the small intestines, what is the halakha? The Gemara elaborates: Here, certainly, since these transgressions come from two different verses, the first minority does not combine with the second minority; or perhaps, since both this transgression and that transgression are the same, eating forbidden fat, the first minority combines with the second minority, and the two minorities together constitute a majority.

Horayot 3a:19.english: And if you say in that case: It is the name of forbidden fat that they both have in common, and the first minority combines with the second minority, then there is another dilemma: In a case where a minority performed a transgression on the basis of the first ruling of the court and ate forbidden fat, and a minority performed a transgression on the basis of the second ruling of the court and ate forbidden blood, what is the halakha? The Gemara elaborates: Here, certainly, they are two distinct prohibitions, and since the nature of their prohibition is not identical, the first minority does not combine with the second minority. Or perhaps, since their offerings are identical, as one is liable to bring a sin-offering for unwitting violation of either of these prohibitions, the first minority combines with the second minority.

Horayot 3a:20.english: And if you say in that case: Since their offerings are identical, the first minority combines with the second minority, then there is another dilemma: In a case where a minority performed a transgression on the basis of the first ruling of the court and ate forbidden fat, and a minority performed a transgression on the basis of the second ruling of the court and engaged in idol worship, what is the halakha? Here, certainly, neither are their prohibitions identical nor are their offerings identical, because an individual who unwittingly engages in idol worship may bring only a female goat for atonement. Therefore, the first minority does not combine with the second minority. Or perhaps, since for both this transgression and that transgression one is liable to receive excision from the World-to-Come [karet] if he performs it intentionally, the first minority combines with the second minority. The Gemara concludes: The dilemma shall stand unresolved.

Horayot 3a:3.english: Up to this point, the Gemara explained the mishna in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda and contrary to the opinion of the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda. And Rav Naḥman says that Shmuel says: The mishna is the statement of Rabbi Meir, but the Rabbis say: An individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the ruling of the court is liable. The Gemara asks: What is the opinion of Rabbi Meir and what is the opinion of the Rabbis to which Shmuel referred? It is as it is taught in a baraita: If the court issued a ruling and the judges performed a transgression on the basis of that ruling, Rabbi Meir deems the judges exempt and the Rabbis deem the judges liable.

Horayot 3a:4.english: The Gemara asks: Who performed the transgression? If we say that it is the members of the court who performed the transgression, what is the reasoning of the Rabbis, who deem the court liable? But isn’t it taught in a baraita: One might have thought that if the court issued a ruling and the members of the court performed the transgression, one might have thought the members of the court would be liable to bring a bull for an unwitting communal sin. The verse states with regard to that bull: “And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation and they performed” (Leviticus 4:13), from which it is derived that the action is dependent on the congregation and the ruling is dependent on the court.

Horayot 3a:5.english: Rather, the case in the baraita is where the court issued a ruling and the majority of the congregation performed a transgression on the basis of that ruling. If so, what is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, who deems the congregation exempt? Rather, is it not referring to a case where the court issued a ruling and a minority of the congregation performed a transgression on the basis of that ruling, and it is with regard to this matter that the tanna’im disagree: One Sage, Rabbi Meir, holds: An individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the ruling of the court is exempt; and one Sage, the Rabbis, holds: An individual who performed a transgression on the basis of a ruling of the court is liable. The mishna, which states that an individual who performs a transgression on the basis of a ruling of the court is exempt, is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir.

Horayot 3a:7.english: Rav Pappa explains: One Sage, the Rabbis, holds: The members of the court combine with the members of the congregation to complete a majority of the congregation. And one Sage, Rabbi Meir, holds: The members of the court do not combine with the members of the congregation to complete a majority of the congregation; therefore, those who sinned on the basis of the ruling of the court constitute less than a majority and the court is exempt from liability to bring an offering. The mishna is not only in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, as in the case of the mishna, but even the Rabbis agree.

Rashi on Horayot 3a:11:1.hebrew: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר אומר משמו: של ר' מאיר והא מתניתא מפרש לקמן.
Rashi on Horayot 3a:11:1.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in his name: In the name of Rabbi Meir, and this Baraita is explained later.

Rashi on Horayot 3a:12:1.english: Rav Asi says: And with regard to a ruling - For we hold that if the court ruled erroneously and the majority of the congregation acted according to their ruling, they bring a bull.

Rashi on Horayot 3a:12:2.english: Follow the majority of its residents in Eretz Yisrael - For those who are outside Eretz Yisrael are not included in the count, nor are those from the Brook of Egypt and beyond, as that is outside Eretz Yisrael.

Rashi on Horayot 3a:13:1.hebrew: פשיטא מרובין ונתמעטו - כגון שהורו בית דין ועשו רוב קהל על פיהם, דנתחייבו להביא פר ולא הספיקו להביא פר עד שנתמעטו שמתו מקצתן; היינו פלוגתא דרבי שמעון ורבנן. דתנן (לקמן הוריות י.) חטא כהן משוח ונשיא עד שלא נתמנו, דהיו חייבים להביא כשבה או שעירה ולא הספיקו להביא עד שנתמנו הרי הן כהדיוטות, ונחייבם להביא כשבה או שעירה כבתחלה. הכא נמי חייבין פר כבתחלה. רבי שמעון אומר וכו': הכא נמי אם נודע להם עד שלא נתמעטו חייבין להביא פר, אבל אם נודע להן משנתמעטו פטורין:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:14:1.hebrew: מועטין ונתרבו מאי - כגון שהורו בית דין ועשו מיעוט קהל על פיהם, דיחיד שעשה בהוראת בית דין פטור. ומתו מקצתן של רוב קהל ונתרבו אלו, ולאחר שנתרבו נודע להם שחטאו. דהני מועטין ונתרבו לא דמי ממש לחטאו עד שלא נתמנו, דמועטין כי חטאו בהוראה לאו בני קרבן נינהו, דיחיד שעשה בהוראת בית דין פטור. אבל כי חטאו כהן משוח ונשיא עד שלא נתמנו, נעשו בני קרבן ומחייבי לאתויי כשבה או שעירה. אבל מרובין ונתמעטו דמי ממש לחטאו עד שלא נתמנו, דהא מרובין כי חטאו בני קרבן נינהו. ואמטול הכי קאמר במרובין ונתמעטו דהוי פלוגתא דרבי שמעון ורבנן. אבל במועטין ונתרבו איבעיא לן אי דמי לפלוגתא דרבי שמעון ורבנן אי לא. מי אמרינן רבי שמעון דבתר ידיעה אזיל דאמר אם נודע להם עד שלא נתמנו חייבין כבתחלה, הכא נמי מחייב דכי אתיידע להו בחיובא אתיידע להו דכי נתרבו אתיידע להו ומביאין פר. ורבנן דבתר חטאה אזלי דאמרי הרי אלו כהדיוטות הואיל וחטאו כי לא נתמנו, הכא נמי אזלי בתר חטאה וכי חטאו אכתי מועטין היו ופטורין, דיחיד שעשה בהוראת בית דין פטור:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:15:1.hebrew: ותסברא אימור דשמעת ליה לרבי שמעון דאזיל אף בתר ידיעה - דאמר אם נודע להם עד שלא נתמנו חייבין היכא דהוי ידיעה וחטאה בחיוב:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:16:1.hebrew: כי השתא - דלהוי כי חטאו משנתמנו, דלייתי פר. ואמאי קתני משנתמנו פטורין? אלא מדקתני פטור, שמע מינה דרבי שמעון חטאה וידיעה בעי בחיובא. ומועטין ונתרבו לדברי הכל פטורין, דכי חטאו בפטור חטאו, דיחיד שעשה בהוראת בית דין פטור:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:17:1.hebrew: או דלמא - כיון דחלב שם אחד הוא, דבין חלב המכסה את הקרב ובין חלב המכסה את הדקין שם אחד הוא, שחלב סתם איקרו:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:19:1.hebrew: כיון דתרי איסורי נינהו - דחלב אינו שוה בכל, דחלב חיה מותר:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:19:2.hebrew: או דלמא - כיון דאילו ציבור אכלי האי חלב והאי דם שלא בהוראה בשגגת מעשה, מייתו כל חד וחד, אי בעו כשבה מייתו אי בעו שעירה מייתו, דמצי אשוויי קרבנם; השתא נמי כי עשו בהוראה מצטרפי:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:20:1.hebrew: ומיעוט בתרא בעבודת כוכבים - קרבנם שעירה ולא כשבה:

Rashi on Horayot 3a:4:1.hebrew: הוראה תלויה בב"ד: דכתיב ונעלם דבר דהיינו שהורו לעבור מעיני הקהל דהיינו ב"ד.
Rashi on Horayot 3a:4:1.english: The ruling is dependent on the court: As it is written: "And the matter is hidden" (Leviticus 4:13), meaning that they ruled to transgress, "from the eyes of the congregation," which refers to the court.

Rashi on Horayot 3a:6:1.hebrew: ב"ד משלים לרוב צבור: דעשו עם מעט צבור והשלימו לרוב צבור.
Rashi on Horayot 3a:6:1.english: The court completes a majority of the congregation: For they acted with a small portion of the congregation and completed a majority of the congregation.

Rashi on Horayot 3a:8:1.hebrew: [צבור מייתי]: ור' מאיר פוטר צבור דהא קא מייתי ב"ד כדאמרי' לקמן רבי מאיר אומר שבעה שבטים שחטאו בית דין מביאין עליהם פר והן פטורין. ואי קשיא הא אמרי' בכל התורה אין מיעוט אחר מיעוט אלא לרבות, והיכי אמרי' אלו ג' מיעוטין דממעטינן אותם? בירושלמי מפרש ה"מ היכא דליכא אלא ב' מעוטין אבל הכא דאיכא ג' מיעוטין בזה אחר זה בחד קרא כולהו אתו למעט וכן בל"ב מדות מצאתי.
Rashi on Horayot 3a:8:1.english: [The congregation brings]: And Rabbi Meir exempts the congregation, for the court brings, as we say later, Rabbi Meir says: If seven tribes sinned, the court brings a bull for them, and they are exempt. And if you ask, we said throughout the Torah that a limitation after a limitation is only to include, so how can we say these are three limitations that we exclude with them? In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is explained that this applies where there are only two limitations, but here, where there are three limitations one after another in one verse, all of them come to exclude. And so I found in the thirty-two rules.

Rashi on Horayot 3a:9:1.hebrew: אותו השבט חייב: להביא פר דקסבר שבט אחד אקרי קהל.
Rashi on Horayot 3a:9:1.english: That tribe is liable: To bring a bull, for Rabbi Yehuda holds that one tribe is called a congregation.

Rashi on Horayot 3b:1:1.hebrew: או לא בעינן ההוא בית דין דהורו להם מעיקרא דתהוי להו ידיעה - כלומר, לא בעינן דתהוי להו ידיעה לבית דין קמא ומצטרפי:

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3a:13.english: Rashi explains that the main comparison is that, according to the Rabbis, the bringing of the offering depends on the state of affairs at the time of the sin, while Rabbi Shimon also takes into account the awareness, according to which they determine which offering the sinners are obligated to bring. See in Ḥafetz Hashem, which explains that the main approach of Rabbi Shimon is based on the assumption that "new circumstances have arisen here," meaning a change occurred in the essence of the sinners, and therefore their law also changes. The same applies to the question here, where the majority became a minority.

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3a:4.english: As it is written: “And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Leviticus 4:13). The court is characterized as the eyes of the congregation (Rashi).

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3a:6.english: In the book Chefetz Hashem, several issues with this reasoning are explored: According to the one who says that the court does not complete a majority of the public, when counting the majority of the public, is the court taken into account, such that there must be a majority of the public even against the court, or not? And it also discusses the question of whether, if the court acted according to their ruling, the majority of the public needs to be greater than the minority when combined with the court, or if the court is not counted at all.

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3b:1.english: There is room to say that only when the court that issued the ruling itself later retracted and decided that it had erred — then the public brings an offering. But the decision of another court would not have this law, rather the congregation would be considered as if they acted due to the error of individuals.

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Horayot 3a:13.english: If those who performed the transgression were numerous at the time of the sin and became a minority at the time the error became known, or if they were few and became a majority at the time of awareness — everything follows the time of the act, in accordance with the words of the Rabbis, and not according to the individual opinion of Rabbi Shimon. (Rambam Sefer

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Horayot 3a:4.english: If the court issued an erroneous ruling and permitted a prohibition for which one is liable to bring a sin-offering for its unwitting violation, and a majority of the people performed the transgression on the basis of the ruling of the court, the court is liable to bring a sin-offering for their erroneous ruling, even if the judges did not perform the transgression. In this matter, the determining factor is the ruling of the court, not its actions (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 12:1).

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:10.english: And if you wish, say the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis in this way: The Baraita discusses a case, for example, where six tribes sinned and they constitute a majority of the congregation in number, or seven tribes sinned even though they are not a majority of the congregation in number. And whose opinion is expressed in our Mishna, the opinion of the Rabbis? It is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:11.english: As it is taught in a Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Meir: If six tribes sinned and they constitute a majority of the congregation, or seven tribes sinned even though they are not a majority of the congregation – they are liable. And from all these refutations, it emerges that there is no proof for the words of Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel that our Mishna is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:12.english: Rav Asi says: And with regard to a ruling, to determine what constitutes the majority of a congregation, one should follow the majority of the children of Israel, only the residents of Eretz Yisrael are the ones who determine this, as it is stated: 'And Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God, seven days and seven days, fourteen days' (I Kings 8:65). And we will clarify what is stated in this verse: Since it is written: 'And all Israel with him,' if so, why do I need 'a great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt'? What does this come to add? Conclude from it: The additional verse comes to teach us that these residents of Eretz Yisrael are called a congregation; but those others who are outside Eretz Yisrael are not called a congregation.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:13.english: And further regarding the matter of the majority of the congregation: It is obvious to us that if those who performed based on the court's ruling were numerous and afterwards diminished, for example, if some of them died and they now became a minority of the congregation — this is the dispute of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis. They disagreed in a mishna later (Horayot 10b) regarding an anointed Kohen or a king who sinned unwittingly before their appointment, and afterwards were appointed to these positions. According to the Rabbis, since they were laymen at the time of their sin, they bring an offering as laymen. Whereas Rabbi Shimon holds that if they became aware of the sin while still laymen, they bring an offering as laymen, but if they became aware after their appointment, they are exempt. According to these views, even in this case of numerous who diminished, the Rabbis will say that since they sinned while being a majority, they bring an offering. And according to Rabbi Shimon, the matter will depend on the time they became aware of the unwitting sin, whether they were a majority or a minority at that time.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:14.english: However, one might ask the opposite: If at the time they sinned they were few and afterwards increased, for example, if some of the majority of the congregation who did not sin died, such that now the minority that sinned constitutes the majority, what is the law? Do Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree on this as well? And in this manner: Rabbi Shimon, who follows the time of awareness, deems them liable, and the Rabbis, who follow the time of the transgression, deem them exempt. Or not? If so, what is the conclusion?

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:15.english: They refute: And can you understand to attribute the law in this case to the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis? Say that you heard Rabbi Shimon, who follows even awareness, and when? In a case where both the awareness and the transgression were in a state of liability, meaning that whether as a layman, a Nasi, or an anointed Kohen, there is some obligation to bring an offering for the sinner. But awareness that was not accompanied by a transgression, did you hear him say that?

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:16.english: For if so, that Rabbi Shimon would also follow only the time of awareness and would obligate in the case of few who increased. Let them bring according to their present status an offering of a Kohen Gadol or a king when they became aware after they were appointed. But why did Rabbi Shimon say that in such a case they are exempt! Rather, it is certain that according to Rabbi Shimon's view, both the transgression and awareness are required. Therefore, there is no solution for the question that was asked.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:17.english: And further, a dilemma was raised before them [the Sages]: If the court issued a ruling that forbidden fat is permitted, and a minority of the congregation performed the transgression of eating fat on the basis of their ruling, and the court reversed their initial ruling, but afterward they reversed themselves again and issued a ruling to permit it, and then a different minority performed the transgression on the basis of their ruling, what is the halakha? The two sides of the question are: Is it that since there are two separate instances of awareness, the first minority does not combine with the second minority, even though these two minorities together constitute a majority of the congregation? Or perhaps, since both this transgression and that transgression are the prohibition of eating forbidden fat, they combine?

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:18.english: And if you say: Since both this transgression and that transgression are the prohibition of eating forbidden fat, they combine, then there is room for the following dilemma: If there was a minority that erred based on one ruling of the court regarding fat that is upon the stomach, and a minority that erred based on another ruling regarding fat that is upon the small intestines, what is the halakha? The two sides of this question are: Here, certainly, since these come from two verses, as each type of fat has a different source in the Torah, the first minority does not combine; or perhaps, since both this transgression and that transgression are the prohibition of eating forbidden fat, and they are included in one prohibition, they combine?

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:19.english: And if you say: It is the name 'fat' and it combines, then there is room for the following dilemma: If a minority of the congregation erred based on a court ruling regarding forbidden fat, and a minority erred based on a ruling regarding forbidden blood, what is the halakha? The two sides of this question are: Here, certainly, since they are two different prohibitions, and since their prohibition is not identical, they do not combine. Or perhaps, since their offerings are identical, as for both of them one brings a sin-offering, they combine?

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:20.english: And if you say: Since their offerings are identical, they combine, another dilemma will arise: If there was a minority that erred based on a ruling regarding forbidden fat, and a different minority that erred regarding idol worship, what is the halakha? The two sides of this question are: Here, certainly, neither are their prohibitions identical nor are their offerings identical, because even an individual who unwittingly engages in idol worship must bring a she-goat specifically for his atonement, so the minorities do not combine. Or perhaps, since both this transgression and that transgression are an offense for which one is liable to receive karet if performed intentionally, there is still a commonality between them, and they combine? These questions were not resolved and the dilemma shall stand unresolved.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:21.english: A dilemma was raised before them [it was asked of them, the students]: If the court issued a ruling that forbidden fat is permitted, and a minority of the congregation performed the transgression on its basis, and that court died and another court stood in its place, and again issued the same ruling to permit, and a different minority performed the transgression, what will be the *halakha*?

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:22.english: And they elaborate: According to the opinion of the one who says that the court alone brings the offering, do not raise the dilemma [do not ask, do not be in doubt] for yourself — as those judges who ruled and on whose basis the majority of the congregation acted are not here, for the first court has already died. Rather, when you should raise the question for yourself — it is according to the opinion of the one who says that the congregation is the one that brings the offering. If so, what [is the *halakha*]? And the sides of the question are: The congregation exists [stands], for together it is found that a majority of the congregation sinned.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:3.english: Up to this point, we have explained our Mishna according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, and the Rabbis disagree with him. But Rav Nachman said Shmuel establishes the Mishna in a different way: This Mishna is the statement of Rabbi Meir, but the Rabbis say: An individual who acted based on the ruling of the court is liable. And they ask: What is that opinion of Rabbi Meir and what is the opinion of the Rabbis to which Shmuel refers? As it is taught in a Baraita: If the court ruled and acted – Rabbi Meir exempts, and the Rabbis obligate.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:4.english: Let us clarify: Who are those who performed the transgression? If you say it was the court, what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who obligate them? But isn't it taught in a Baraita: One might have thought that if the court ruled and the court members themselves performed the transgression, they might be liable to bring a bull for an unwitting communal sin? The verse states: "And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation and they performed" (Leviticus 4:13), to say that the action is dependent on the congregation and the ruling is dependent on the court!

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:5.english: Rather, you should explain that the intention is: The court issued a ruling and the majority of the congregation performed a transgression. If so, what is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir who exempts them? Rather, is it not referring to a case where the court issued a ruling and a minority of the congregation performed a transgression, and it is with regard to this matter that they disagree: One Sage, Rabbi Meir, holds: An individual (and similarly a minority of the congregation) who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling is exempt; and one Sage, the Rabbis, holds: An individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling is liable. And from here, it follows that our Mishna, which states that an individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling is exempt, is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:6.english: Rav Pappa said: From here, there is no proof for our matter. For it is possible to explain the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis in the Baraita in another way: Everyone agrees that an individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling is exempt. Rather, Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree on the question of whether the court itself completes a majority of the congregation, in a case where those who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling were not a majority of the public, but if the court itself (who ruled and acted) is added to them, it would be a majority.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:7.english: One Sage, the Rabbis, holds: The court completes a majority of the congregation, and therefore the public is liable. And one Sage, Rabbi Meir, holds: The court does not complete a majority of the congregation, and this is considered like an individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling and is exempt. If so, our Mishna is not necessarily in accordance with Rabbi Meir.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:8.english: And if you wish, say and explain the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis in this way: The Baraita speaks of a case where the court issued a ruling and a majority of the congregation performed a transgression, and the court is liable to bring a bull, and therefore Rabbi Meir exempts the public from bringing an offering. And who are the Rabbis who obligate? This is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, who said: The congregation brings and the court brings the offering.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:9.english: And if you wish, say this in explaining the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis: It deals with the law of one tribe that performed a transgression on the basis of its court's ruling. According to Rabbi Meir, the law of "unwitting communal sin" does not apply to a tribal court, and therefore the court is exempt from an offering. And who are the Rabbis who obligate? It is the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, as it is taught in a Baraita: A tribe that performed a transgression on the basis of its court's ruling, that tribe is liable.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:1.english: Or perhaps [maybe] we require [we need] the awareness of that court that issued the ruling; and that court no longer exists! This question was not resolved and remained as a *teiku* [it shall stand] in its place.

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:12:1.english: A great congregation from the entrance of Hamath - Even though we do not derive matters of Torah law from the words of the Prophets, this is merely a clarification of a matter.

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:14:1.hebrew: מועטין ונתרבו מאי - פירש רש"י (בעלמא) [בעיין] דהני לאו בני קרבן כמו משיח ונשיא, אבל מרובין ונתמעטו כבר הוו בני קרבן. ולא נהירא, דאפילו מרובין ונתמעטו, כי נתמעטו לאו בני קרבן נינהו, אם לא דבתר חטאה אזלינן. אבל התם תרוייהו בני קרבן נינהו. אלא משום הכי מבעיא ליה במועטין ונתרבו, דאיכא למימר דאפילו רבי שמעון מודה דפטור כדפירש ואזיל:

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:18:1.hebrew: הורו בית דין שחלב המכסה את הקרב כו' - תימה, דאמרינן לקמן (הוריות ד.) אין בית דין חייבין עד שיורו בדבר שאין הצדוקין מודין; ובשלמא חלב שעל הדקין דאתי מריבויה (חולין מט) ניחא, דאין הצדוקין מודין בו; אלא חלב המכסה את הקרב וכן דם, מאי איכא למימר? מיהו לפי התוספתא דמכילתין ניחא, דתנא לקיים מצות חייבין כיצד יש חלב ודם בתורה, אבל אין חייבין אלא על הקרב לשלמים. ואף על גב דדם חיה נאסר, שמא הצדוקים אומרים דגם הוא קרב:

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:19:1.hebrew: וחזרו והורו שדם מותר - הא דקתני כהאי גוונא, דמשמע דוקא משום שידעו בינתים שטעו בחלב; דהא אפילו לא ידעו נמי מצינן למבעי כדקאמר, משום דשני מינים הם, דם שוה בכל ולא חלב, אלא נקטינן אגב אחריני. והא דלא פשיט מההוא דלעיל עד שיהיו כולן בשגגה אחת, דהכא כיון דתליא בבית דין הוי שגגה אחת:

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:20:1.hebrew: והורו שעבודת כוכבים מותרת - צריך עיון מה יביאו, כיון שאין קרבנותיהן שוין, אם יביאו קרבן עבודת כוכבים וגם דחלב או לא? וגם צריך עיון אי דוקא מיבעיא דמעיקרא הוי מיעוט וכן בסוף, אבל אי הוי רובו בסוף לא איצטרכי למיעוטא שיתכפר בפר לההוא מיעוטא. איכא דאמרי לא שנא, אבל הא ודאי אי הוי מתחלה רובא ולבסוף מיעוטא, אין מיעוט מצטרף לרובא כיון שכבר נתחייבו רובא בקרבן:

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:22:1.hebrew: אלא כי תיבעי לך כו' - צריך עיון: האם היה אפשר לשאול גם לשיטת מאן דאמר בית דין מייתי אם מתו מיעוט ציבור הראשונים ולא נודע כי אם אל אלו החיים, האם אומרים בית דין [חייבים] דמכל מקום הם הורו שלא כדת או לא? והא דנקט מת בית דין ולא נקט הורו בית דין אחר, דלא אפשר כי אם בסנהדרי גדולה:

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:5:1.hebrew: ר"מ סבר יחיד שעשה בהוראת ב"ד פטור: תימה מאי דוחקי' לכך? דלמא ר"מ ס"ל דדוקא יחיד שעשה חייב אבל שנים ושלשה שעשו פטורים, ולית ליה ברייתא דועדיין אני אומר כו' דבלא"ה לית ליה דברייתא אית לה יחיד שעשה בהוראת ב"ד חייב ור"מ אית ליה דפטור. ומיהו כיון דלא מצינו תנא דמחלק בין א' לשנים דחיק למימר הכי.
Tosafot on Horayot 3a:5:1.english: Rabbi Meir holds that an individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling is exempt: It is puzzling, what is the compulsion for this? Perhaps Rabbi Meir holds that specifically an individual who performed a transgression is liable, but two or three who performed a transgression are exempt, and he does not accept the Baraita that states "Still I say" etc., for even without it, he does not accept that Baraita which states that an individual who performed a transgression on the basis of the court's ruling is liable, while Rabbi Meir holds that he is exempt. However, since we do not find a Tanna who distinguishes between one and two, it is difficult to say this.
